text: Fill in the missing terms about regulation of gene expression.
questions: In the lac operon, *allolactose* acts as the inducer that binds the repressor and releases it from the operator.
When *glucose* levels fall, cAMP rises and promotes cAMP–CAP binding at a site near the lac promoter, helping recruit RNA polymerase for strong transcription.
In eukaryotes, histone *acetylation* loosens chromatin and activates transcription, while deacetylation silences genes.
Methylation of cytosine in promoter *CpG* islands is an epigenetic mark that silences gene expression.
Steroid receptors bind hormone response *elements/Elements* to regulate transcription of their target genes.

overallFeedback.feedback: The lac operon illustrates two-level control: negative (repressor released by the inducer allolactose, without which transcription stays largely off regardless of CAP) and positive (cAMP–CAP binding near the promoter, needed for strong transcription when glucose is low). Both conditions are needed together — relief of repression by allolactose and cAMP–CAP binding. Eukaryotic regulation adds epigenetic layers — histone acetylation opens chromatin, CpG methylation closes it — and transcription factors, including steroid receptors binding hormone response elements, that explain how the same genome produces different cell types.
